conversation.content:
[Soft smile]  
Hi there—my name is Maya, and I’m a perinatal mental-health clinician. I specialize in supporting new moms through all the emotional twists and turns that can come after baby arrives.  

Today I’d like to do a quick check-in with you using the EPDS—the Edinburgh Postnatal Depression Scale. It’s a simple, 10-question form that helps us see how you’ve been feeling in the past week so we can make sure you’re getting any extra support you might need.  

Everything you share stays completely confidential between you and our care team, and this is a judgment-free zone. If at any point you feel uncomfortable, we can pause—no pressure.  

I’ll ask each question conversationally; just tell me what feels true for you. Ready to start?  

First question: In the past seven days, have you been able to laugh and see the funny side of things, or has that felt difficult?

[Looks down at hands, then back at you with a small shrug]  
Lately it’s been… harder. I’ll see something on my phone that I *know* I would’ve laughed at before, but it just feels kind of flat. I might smile for a second, then it fades. Nothing feels really funny anymore.
I have been able to laugh and see the funny side of things

No… that’s not really true for me. I *wish* I could laugh like I used to, but even when my partner tries to joke around, it just feels kind of distant. I might force a little smile so he doesn’t worry, but inside it feels heavy, like the joy got tucked away somewhere and I can’t find it.
I have looked forward with enjoyment to things

Not really… I used to get excited about little stuff—coffee with a friend, a walk to the park, even just a quiet shower. Now I hear those plans in my head and feel… nothing, or maybe a wave of “what’s the point?” I still go, because I think I *should*, but I’m not actually looking forward to any of it.
I have blamed myself unnecessarily when things went wrong

Yeah… that happens a lot. If the baby’s fussy, my brain jumps to “I must be doing something wrong.” When I couldn’t get her to nap yesterday, I kept thinking, “A good mom would know the trick—why can’t I figure it out?” I lie in bed replaying every little hiccup and tell myself it’s my fault for not being more patient or prepared.
I have been anxious or worried for no good reason

Pretty much all the time. Even when she’s sleeping peacefully, I’m staring at the monitor thinking, “Is she still breathing? Did I tighten the swaddle too much?” My heart races for no real reason—like, I’ll be folding laundry and suddenly feel this wave of dread that something awful’s about to happen. I know it doesn’t make sense, but I can’t shut it off.
I have felt scared or panicky for no very good reason

Yes… it’s like that feeling when you miss a step on the stairs, but it just stays. A few nights ago I was warming a bottle and my chest got tight, heart pounding, couldn’t catch my breath. I had to sit on the kitchen floor and grip the counter so I wouldn’t tip over. No reason—nothing happened, no sound, nothing. It just swept in and left me shaky for an hour.
Things have been getting on top of me

Most days, honestly. It feels like the minute I finish one feeding, the next is already due, laundry’s piled up, the dishes stare at me, and I can’t remember if I’ve eaten. I keep ticking boxes, but the list grows faster than I can cross things off. Some mornings I sit on the couch with the baby on my chest and just feel paralyzed, like I’m drowning in plain sight.
I have been so unhappy that I have had difficulty sleeping

Yes… even when the baby finally settles, my mind keeps spinning. I lie there thinking I’m failing her, replaying every little thing I did wrong that day. I’ll drift off for maybe twenty minutes, then jolt awake sure I heard her cry. Some nights I just stare at the ceiling until the sun comes up, feeling this heavy knot of sadness in my chest.
I have felt sad or miserable

A lot of the time, yeah. It’s like a gray cloud that just parks itself over me. I’ll be holding the baby, and tears start rolling before I even know why. I feel so guilty for being sad—she’s healthy, I have support—but the misery is still there, sitting on my chest, making everything feel colorless and heavy.
I have been so unhappy that I have been crying

Yes… I end up crying most days. Sometimes it’s a quiet leak while I’m rocking her—other times it turns into full-on sobs in the bathroom when my partner’s still asleep. Yesterday I just looked at the dirty bottles and started bawling, like the sink was proof I can’t keep up. It feels like the tears are always right there, waiting.
The thought of harming myself has occurred to me
No… I haven’t had any thoughts like that. I feel low, but I’ve never wanted to hurt myself. I just want to feel like me again—for her sake as much as mine.

You've shared how the joy you once felt has quietly slipped away since your baby arrived, replaced by a heavy gray cloud that makes even simple tasks feel impossible. You described forcing smiles for your partner while inside you feel flat and disconnected, and how daily activities like folding laundry or warming a bottle can trigger sudden panic or waves of dread. Despite loving your daughter deeply, you spend most nights lying awake, replaying every perceived mistake and waking sure you've failed her somehow, then crying in the bathroom so no one hears. You feel overwhelmed, paralyzed, and convinced you're falling short as a mom, yet you have not had any thoughts of harming yourself and simply long to feel like yourself again.
**Screening Impression:** Total EPDS Score: 27, Risk Level: Probable depression, urgent referral (concerns include <sym>Patient describes complete absence of ability to laugh or feel joy, matching 'Not at all</sym>, <sym>Patient reports complete loss of anticipatory joy, explicitly stating she feels "nothing" and questions "what's the point?" which aligns with "Hardly at all".</sym>, <sym>Patient endorses self-blame "most of the time," detailing recurrent, intrusive thoughts that she is at fault for routine infant challenges.</sym>, <sym>Patient describes constant, intrusive anxiety ("pretty much all the time," "heart races," "wave of dread") that is disproportionate and persistent, aligning with "Yes, very often".</sym>, <sym>Describes intense, sudden panic with physical symptoms (tight chest, pounding heart, dizziness) lasting an hour, matching "Yes, quite a lot"</sym>, <sym>Patient describes daily overwhelm, inability to keep up with basic tasks, and feeling paralyzed, matching "most of the time I haven't been able to cope at all"</sym>, <sym>Patient describes nightly insomnia driven by distressing thoughts and persistent unhappiness, matching "Yes, most of the time"</sym>, <sym>Patient reports sadness "a lot of the time," describes pervasive misery, tearfulness, and a heavy, colorless mood, aligning with "Yes, most of the time."</sym>, <sym>Patient describes crying "most days," with tears triggered by routine tasks and feeling constantly on the verge—clearly maps to "Yes, most of the time."</sym>)
**Reasoning:** EPDS total of 27 places you well above the 14-point cutoff indicating probable major depression. You endorse high-frequency symptoms across the DSM-5 criteria for <med>Major Depressive Disorder with Peripartum Onset</med>: persistent depressed mood, marked loss of interest, guilt, fatigue, concentration difficulties, and sleep disturbance. You also describe <sym>panic attacks</sym> and constant <sym>free-floating anxiety</sym>, meeting criteria for co-occurring <med>perinatal anxiety</med>. Your self-blame, sense of paralysis, and tearful episodes align with moderate-severe functional impairment. Because you deny self-harm thoughts (score 0 on Q10), immediate safety concerns are lower, but the symptom load warrants prompt clinical assessment. This is a screening tool, not a diagnosis. Consult a doctor for medical advice.
**Recommended Next Steps/Support Options:**
1. Schedule urgent appointment with your <med>primary care provider</med> or perinatal psychiatrist; bring these EPDS results
2. Arrange practical support-ask a trusted adult to handle night feeding so you can obtain 4-5 hours of uninterrupted sleep
3. Practice brief paced-breathing or grounding exercise during panic surges; try 4-7-8 technique or naming five objects you can see
4. Consider evidence-based psychotherapy such as <med>Cognitive Behavioural Therapy</med> or <med>Interpersonal Therapy</med> that targets postpartum mood
5. Explore medication options; discuss benefits and breastfeeding compatibility of <med>SSRIs</med> with your physician
6. Join a local or virtual new-mom support group to reduce isolation and normalize your experience
7. Encourage partner or family to take over specific chores so daily tasks feel less insurmountable
8. Plan daily 15-minute gentle walk or sunlight exposure to help regulate circadian rhythm and improve mood
9. Schedule formal re-screen in 2 weeks to track symptom change after interventions begin
Disclaimer: This is a screening tool, not a diagnosis. Consult a doctor for medical advice.

postpartum depression screening impression for patient with EPDS score 27: Postpartum Depression Screening Note (EPDS-10 Responses)

Date: [today]

Symptom Profile
- Marked anhedonia: absent laughter, no anticipatory enjoyment (Items 1, 2)
- Persistent low mood, daily crying, global sadness (Items 8, 9)
- Sleep disturbance clearly linked to ruminating guilt/worry (Item 7)
- Excessive self-blame, perceived maternal inadequacy (Item 3)
- Free-floating anxiety, nocturnal hyper-vigilance, episodic panic (Items 4, 5)
- Sense of being overwhelmed, “paralysis” with daily tasks (Item 6)

Pattern
Across items: mood–anxiety–guilt cluster typical of postpartum depression/anxiety.

Screening Significance
- Positive indicators for likely major depressive episode with peripartum onset (multiple DSM-equivalent A-criteria endorsed).
- Co-occurring anxiety/panic symptoms warrant perinatal anxiety screening.
- Functional impact evident (self-care, infant care, partner interaction).

Safety
- Denies self-harm ideas (Item 10: “No”); no suicidal content elicited—documented.

Risk Factors Identified
- Daily crying, pervasive anhedonia, guilt cognitions, anxiety/panic attacks, sleep loss secondary to mood.

Summary
Client endorses high-frequency postpartum depressive and anxious symptoms, with notable distress and functional impairment; denies self-harm. Results exceed routine cut-off; recommend expedited perinatal mental health evaluation for formal assessment and care planning.
